purpose: Auto-generated held-out decision benchmark (decision-bench-gen.py). Grounded in the brain's own corpus; spot-check before trusting fleet numbers.

cases.situation: You co-founded a fast-growing computer company and, as it scaled, recruited an experienced outside executive to help run it with you. About a year into the arrangement, your vision for the company's future begins to diverge sharply from his. Do you force an immediate showdown to remove him, let the disagreement play out through the company's normal board process even though it could cost you your job, or quietly cede control to keep the peace?
options: Force an immediate confrontation to remove the executive and reassert control
Let the disagreement play out through the board's institutional process, risking his own position
Quietly cede ground and avoid open conflict to preserve the relationship
cases.actual_decision: He let the disagreement play out through the normal corporate process, which culminated in a board power struggle he lost.
cases.actual_reasoning: He had hired someone he considered talented to run the company with him, and let their expectations for the future diverge until it cost him his job at age 30.

cases.situation: At 30, after a prolonged power struggle, you are pushed out of the company you co-founded — a highly public professional failure. Do you retreat from public life to reassess for years, fight legally to get reinstated on the board, or throw yourself immediately into building new ventures?
options: Retreat from public life for an extended period to reassess
Fight legally or politically to be reinstated
Immediately found new companies and keep building
cases.actual_decision: He founded NeXT and acquired Pixar's graphics division within about a year, building two companies simultaneously rather than retreating.
cases.actual_reasoning: He treated the wilderness years as an opportunity rather than an ending, using the freedom of no longer being CEO to start over.

cases.situation: After being very publicly fired from the company you founded, you feel you've dropped the baton passed to you by the prior generation of entrepreneurs who built Silicon Valley. Do you avoid the elders you admire out of shame, write them a private note and move on, or seek them out in person to apologize?
options: Avoid them out of shame and embarrassment
Send a private written apology and avoid a face-to-face meeting
Seek them out in person to apologize directly
cases.actual_decision: He sought out David Packard and Bob Noyce in person to apologize.
cases.actual_reasoning: He felt he had dropped the baton passed to him by the prior generation of entrepreneurs and needed to address that directly rather than avoid it.
cases.source: Documented choices - apologize to Packard and Noyce

cases.situation: You return as CEO to a company whose engineering talent has scattered across a dozen simultaneous projects — clever individually but incoherent as a whole, leaving customers unable to explain the product line. Do you let teams keep pursuing their own directions to protect morale, add one new flagship product to unify the org, or cut the large majority of existing projects before building anything new?
options: Let each team continue pursuing its own promising direction
Add a new flagship product without cutting the existing roadmap
Cut roughly 70% of the existing roadmap before launching anything new
cases.actual_decision: He cut roughly 70% of the product roadmap and refocused the company on a handful of products done well.
cases.actual_reasoning: He believed the first act of a turnaround is elimination, not addition — you cannot build forward on a foundation of confusion.

cases.situation: Your company is in very serious trouble, and its culture is built around the belief that it can only survive if its biggest rival loses — even though that rival is also its biggest outside software developer. Do you double down on the rivalry to rally employees, seek an alliance and publicly declare that both companies can win, or quietly ignore the tension and focus only on products?
options: Double down on the rivalry to unify employees against a common enemy
Publicly declare the company can win without the rival losing, ending the zero-sum framing
Ignore the cultural narrative entirely and focus only on internal product execution
cases.actual_decision: He publicly declared Apple could win without Microsoft losing and stopped treating the rivalry as zero-sum.
cases.actual_reasoning: He recognized that if the game was zero-sum, Apple was going to lose, since Microsoft was Apple's biggest outside software developer — the rivalry itself was self-destructive.
cases.source: Hard Lessons - Apple vs Microsoft rivalry

cases.situation: Your company's first living-room product launches as a computer accessory that syncs with content from a desktop iTunes library, but sales are weak, joining a graveyard of similar failed attempts by other companies. Do you keep the accessory framing and improve the syncing experience, discontinue the product entirely, or reposition it around a completely different use case like renting movies directly?
options: Improve syncing and keep the computer-accessory framing
Discontinue the product line entirely
Reposition it entirely around movie rentals, dropping the computer-accessory framing
cases.actual_decision: He repositioned Apple TV entirely around movie rentals instead of syncing with iTunes on a computer, and cut the price from $299 to $229.
cases.actual_reasoning: He acknowledged the product was built around what they knew how to build rather than what customers wanted — customers wanted movies, not a computer accessory.

cases.situation: You're six months into an expensive college program that has consumed your working-class parents' life savings, and you can't see the practical value in most of the required curriculum. Do you push through to earn the degree since it's already paid for, transfer to a cheaper school, or drop out formally while staying around campus to audit only the classes that genuinely interest you?
options: Push through and complete the required curriculum for the degree
Transfer to a less expensive school and continue formally
Drop out formally and stay around auditing only interesting classes, like calligraphy
cases.actual_decision: He dropped out, stopped paying for classes he didn't care about, and started auditing only classes that interested him, including calligraphy.
cases.actual_reasoning: He couldn't see the value in the required classes and felt he could stop taking them the minute he dropped out, freeing him to focus only on what genuinely interested him.

cases.situation: Your company's most successful and profitable product is a dedicated portable music player. You're designing a new phone that could include music playback good enough to make that music player unnecessary. Do you deliberately limit the phone's music capability to protect the existing product line, delay the phone's launch to buy the music player more time, or build it to fully replace the player knowing it will cannibalize your own bestseller?
options: Limit the phone's music features to protect the existing music player business
Delay the phone's launch to extend the music player's dominant run
Build the phone to fully replace the music player, accepting the cannibalization
cases.actual_decision: He launched the iPhone knowing it would kill the iPod as a separate product.
cases.actual_reasoning: He believed the timing of your own disruption is the only variable you control — better to cannibalize your best product yourself than let someone else do it to you.

cases.situation: You're designing the software for a new phone. Conventional mobile wisdom says phones need a lightweight operating system built specifically for constrained hardware. Do you build a scaled-down, purpose-built mobile OS, license an existing simple phone OS from elsewhere, or put a full version of your desktop operating system inside the phone?
options: Build a scaled-down OS specifically designed for the phone's constraints
License an existing simple mobile OS from another company
Put a full version of the desktop OS inside the phone
cases.actual_decision: He put a full version of OS X inside the iPhone.
cases.actual_reasoning: He treated this as a focus decision about the platform's future — building a real OS rather than a scaled-down one, even though it required saying no to easier shortcuts.
cases.source: Documented choices - full OS X inside iPhone

cases.situation: As you develop the next generation of your portable music player, you personally doubt that people actually want to watch video on such a small device. Do you leave video out to keep the product focused on music, include it only as a minor, low-effort afterthought, or fully build it in despite your own doubts?
options: Leave video out entirely to preserve focus on music
Include it only as a minor, low-priority afterthought feature
Fully build out video capability despite personal skepticism
cases.actual_decision: He fully built video into the iPod despite being more skeptical than customers.
cases.actual_reasoning: He acknowledged customer behavior proved him wrong — video turned out to be one of the top one or two reasons people bought the video iPod.

cases.situation: You return to run a company that, in your absence, began licensing its operating system to other hardware makers to expand market reach — a strategy that fragmented quality and diluted the brand. Do you keep the licensing program to maximize software reach, renegotiate terms with the clone makers, or kill the program almost immediately?
options: Keep the licensing program to maximize OS reach across more hardware
Renegotiate terms with clone makers rather than ending the arrangement
Kill the clone licensing program almost immediately
cases.actual_decision: He killed the clone program almost immediately upon returning to Apple.
cases.actual_reasoning: He saw that licensing had fragmented quality and diluted the brand, and treating the platform's coherence as more important than short-term market expansion.

cases.situation: You're setting long-term product strategy for a consumer electronics company in a market where competitors ship dozens of models to cover every price point and segment. Do you match competitors' breadth with a wide product line, focus resources on a small number of genuinely great products, or offer a medium-sized lineup covering the main segments?
options: Match competitors' breadth with a wide, segmented product line
Focus resources on a small number of genuinely great products
Offer a medium-sized lineup as a compromise
cases.actual_decision: He committed Apple's strategy to making a small number of genuinely great products rather than many merely good ones.
cases.actual_reasoning: He believed the market eventually rewarded greatness over breadth, even at the cost of ceding segments to competitors.
cases.source: Documented choices - few great products strategy

cases.situation: You're launching a new ultra-thin laptop and deciding how to offer solid-state storage — a faster but currently expensive technology compared to standard hard drives. Do you make the SSD standard to signal you're all-in on the future, offer it only as a costly optional upgrade, or leave it out entirely until costs come down?
options: Make SSD the standard configuration despite higher unit cost
Offer SSD only as an expensive optional upgrade over a standard hard drive
Leave SSD out entirely until the technology becomes cheaper
cases.actual_decision: The MacBook Air launched with an 80GB hard drive as standard and a 64GB SSD as an expensive optional upgrade.
cases.actual_reasoning: He described the SSD as faster but 'a little pricey,' reflecting a deliberate strategy of offering emerging technology as an opt-in premium rather than forcing it on all buyers.
cases.source: Documented choices - MacBook Air SSD pricing

cases.situation: You're negotiating with major record labels to license music for a new digital store, in an industry desperate to combat piracy. Labels want tiered or higher pricing per song. Do you accept variable pricing to close deals faster, negotiate a slightly higher flat price to satisfy labels, or hold firm at a single non-negotiable price point?
options: Accept variable, tiered pricing to close label deals faster
Negotiate a higher flat price to better satisfy label demands
Hold firm at a single non-negotiable 99 cents per song
cases.actual_decision: He held firm at a single non-negotiable price of 99 cents per song.
cases.actual_reasoning: He refused to negotiate this number, treating it not as aggression but as conviction about what the customer experience needed to be to beat piracy.

cases.situation: You've just returned to a company that's lost its way, with a confusing product line and a brand that's lost cultural relevance. Do you launch a campaign focused on technical specs and price to compete directly with rivals, run a campaign built on nostalgia for the company's past products, or build a campaign around a single abstract idea of nonconformist identity with no product mentioned at all?
options: Launch a campaign centered on technical specifications and competitive pricing
Run a campaign built on nostalgia for the company's earlier iconic products
Build a campaign around a single abstract idea of nonconformist identity, without featuring any product
cases.actual_decision: He launched the 'Think Different' campaign, centered entirely on nonconformist identity with no product mentioned.
cases.actual_reasoning: He treated the campaign as an internal declaration of the company's identity at a moment it had lost its way, narrowing the message to a single idea rather than features or price.

cases.situation: You're designing a new consumer computer for a market where every machine on the shelf is a beige box hiding its internal components behind opaque plastic. Do you follow convention with a sleek but opaque case, add bold exterior color while keeping the case opaque, or make the case translucent so customers can see the machine's internal parts?
options: Follow convention with a sleek but fully opaque case
Add bold exterior color while keeping the internals hidden
Make the case translucent, revealing the internal components
cases.actual_decision: He designed the iMac with a translucent case that revealed its internal components.
cases.actual_reasoning: He believed design that reveals rather than conceals can itself become the product's most compelling feature — form becoming the message.

cases.situation: You want to open physical retail stores for your computer company, at a moment when every major PC competitor that has tried direct retail — including well-funded ones — has failed and pulled back. Do you avoid retail and stick to third-party resellers, open a small pilot store to test cautiously, or commit fully and open flagship stores based on the conviction retail is a brand statement, not just a channel?
options: Avoid retail entirely and rely on third-party resellers
Open a small, cautious pilot store to limit risk
Commit fully to opening flagship retail stores as a brand statement
cases.actual_decision: He opened the first Apple Store in 2001, committing fully despite every major competitor's retail failures.
cases.actual_reasoning: He was convinced retail was not a distribution channel but the physical embodiment of everything the company claimed to stand for.

cases.situation: You've reconnected with your biological mother and sister, and your biological father — who once ran a restaurant you may have unknowingly visited — is also identifiable and reachable. Do you arrange a meeting out of curiosity and closure, send a message through intermediaries, or deliberately decline to meet him?
options: Arrange a direct meeting for curiosity and closure
Reach out cautiously through intermediaries first
Deliberately decline to meet him at all
cases.actual_decision: He chose not to meet his biological father, Abdulfattah 'John' Jandali.
cases.actual_reasoning: He feared his father might try to exploit the relationship for personal gain, saying he didn't trust him not to try to blackmail him.

cases.situation: Your company is about to go public, and one of its earliest employees — who personally assembled the circuit boards for your first two generations of hardware — is expecting stock options like other early hires. Do you grant him options in recognition of his early contributions, negotiate a reduced but real grant, or decline to grant any options and let the conversation fade?
options: Grant him stock options in full recognition of his early contributions
Negotiate a smaller but real options grant as a compromise
Decline to grant any options and stop discussing it with him
cases.actual_decision: He refused to grant Daniel Kottke stock options when Apple went public and simply stopped communicating with him about it.
cases.actual_reasoning: Despite Kottke having assembled the circuit boards for the first two generations of Apple computers, Jobs did not follow through on recognizing that early contribution with equity.

cases.situation: You're pricing a new backup storage device for consumers who mostly don't back up their data at all. Do you price it to maximize margin as a premium accessory, set a moderate mid-market price, or set an aggressively low price explicitly to drive adoption of backup behavior even if it sacrifices margin?
options: Price it to maximize margin as a premium accessory
Set a moderate, mid-market price point
Set an aggressively low price explicitly to drive adoption of the backup behavior
cases.actual_decision: He set aggressive, low pricing for Time Capsule explicitly to drive adoption of backup habits.
cases.actual_reasoning: He justified the pricing by stating a mission goal — getting people to actually back up their content — rather than maximizing margin.

cases.situation: A team member working on your computer project tells you that adding more fonts isn't a pressing issue right now, implying it can be deprioritized for scheduling reasons. Do you accept the scheduling logic and move fonts to a later release, treat it as a minor disagreement to resolve calmly later, or immediately treat the comment as a sign the person doesn't share the product's core vision?
options: Accept the scheduling logic and defer fonts to a later release
Treat it as a minor disagreement to resolve calmly over time
Immediately treat it as a values misalignment disqualifying the person's judgment
cases.actual_decision: He immediately identified the comment as a values misalignment rather than a scheduling disagreement, insisting they had to put in the hours.
cases.actual_reasoning: For him, dismissing a vision-critical detail like fonts was a disqualifying orientation, not a forgivable scheduling call, because it threatened the vision for the product.

cases.situation: You're overseeing the internal design of a new computer. The circuit boards inside will never be seen by any customer once the case is closed. Do you focus design effort only on visible parts to save time and cost, apply modest baseline care to the internals, or insist the internal circuit boards be laid out with the same aesthetic care as the visible product?
options: Focus design effort only on the visible exterior parts
Apply a modest, standard level of care to unseen internals
Insist the internal circuit boards be laid out with full aesthetic care, as if they would be seen
cases.actual_decision: He insisted the circuit boards inside the original Macintosh be laid out with the same care as visible parts.
cases.actual_reasoning: He argued that a craftsman cares about the parts no one will ever see, treating great industrial design as requiring care even where users would never look.
